title: When Galileo Calculated the Precise Dimensions of Hell in Dante’s Inferno

body:
in History, Literature, Religion, Science |   	September 21st, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			
We ven­er­ate Galileo Galilei for dar­ing to speak the sci­en­tif­ic truth in the face of severe insti­tu­tion­al oppo­si­tion. He pub­licly acknowl­edged that the Earth revolves around the Sun in a time when the Church would rather he did­n’t, dis­play­ing a bloody-mind­ed­ness that he seems to have acquired with age. Decades ear­li­er, in the first stage of his career, he found him­self (cir­ca 1588) tasked by the Flo­ren­tine Acad­e­my with cal­cu­lat­ing the pre­cise dimen­sions of hell as described in Dan­te’s Divine Com­e­dy. Duti­ful­ly apply­ing him­self to this now-absurd-sound­ing work, he deter­mined that the under­world’s roof had to be cen­tered in Jerusalem, as wide as the radius of the entire Earth, and no less than 600 kilo­me­ters thick.
Not that any of this was based on friv­o­lous rea­son­ing. As a mod­el for the dimen­sions of hel­l’s roof, for instance, Galileo looked over to Fil­ip­po Brunelleschi’s dome, which had topped the Flo­rence Cathe­dral for a cen­tu­ry and a half at that point. Galileo’s cal­cu­la­tions of hel­l’s dimen­sions con­tra­dict­ed an ear­li­er mod­el pro­posed by the schol­ar Alessan­dro Vel­lutel­lo. Instead, they sup­port­ed a mod­el devel­oped by archi­tect Anto­nio Manet­ti, whose draw­ings appear here.
That Manet­ti was a fel­low Flo­ren­tine, and Vel­lutel­lo was from Flo­rence’s long­time rival Luc­ca could well have count­ed among the moti­vat­ing fac­tors. But we must bear in mind that, in the six­teenth cen­tu­ry, peo­ple real­ly did want to get these facts straight — if “facts” be the prop­er term.

The attempt to rec­on­cile scrip­ture with objec­tiv­i­ty absorbed the lives of many high­ly intel­li­gent peo­ple through­out the Mid­dle Ages and the Renais­sance. How­ev­er hope­less that goal could be, the thought Galileo devot­ed to the prob­lem may have result­ed in a gen­uine break­through. Math­e­mati­cian and sci­ence his­to­ri­an Mark Peter­son, pre­vi­ous­ly fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture, has argued that his cal­cu­la­tions of Dan­te’s non-Euclid­ean, topol­o­gy-curved uni­verse — as we might plau­si­bly describe it today — laid out the basis for what would become math­e­mat­i­cal physics. In any case, the young Galileo’s lec­tures at the Flo­ren­tine Acad­e­my land­ed him a job as a math­e­mat­ics lec­tur­er at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Pisa, as good a rea­son as any for him to keep his pri­vate doubts to him­self. When it comes to sci­ence and reli­gion, as he must have known, you’ve got to pick your bat­tles.
Relat­ed con­tent:

Based in Seoul, Col­in Marshall writes and broad­casts on cities, lan­guage, and cul­ture. He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

body:
Before he became a nov­el­ist, Haru­ki Muraka­mi ran a jazz bar in Tokyo, and music has filled his nov­els ever since. For your lis­ten­ing plea­sure, NTS Radio has cre­at­ed two playlists of the jazz and clas­si­cal music ref­er­enced in his fic­tion. Togeth­er, they run near­ly five hours and fea­ture every­one from John Coltrane, Bill Evans, and Thelo­nious Monk to Schu­bert, Liszt, and Mozart. Our sug­ges­tion: Pick up a Muraka­mi nov­el, press play, and let the music become the sound­track to your read­ing. Enjoy!

title: The Cathedral of Joy
description:

body:
Weekly Newsletter
								One-on-one with Alfredo Jaar, Damien Hirst’s secret life, Anish Kapoor's optical trickery, and another BS "most influential" list.  
						
								
																
														
								
						
		
	  		    
        
    
		
				
						At a cafe named Anti Cafe — though it looks like any other cafe — a man is writing dozens of cards by hand, sealing them inside pretty little envelopes, and stacking them in a pile on the table. After half an hour of observing him from the next table, I finally ask, “Are those wedding invitations?” “Nope,” he replies.“Birthday party invitations?”“Nope.”“So what are they for, if you don’t mind me asking?”“Just letters to my friends to show them how much I appreciate them,” he discloses with an air of self-satisfaction. “Oh, that’s so beautiful,” I say with my hand on my heart, feeling sincerely touched. But as I leave the cafe, I begin wondering if that guy is okay. Down in the subway station, I see another young man using a Sharpie pen to make meticulous drawings of the Manhattan grid on a large piece of cardboard. Avenue by avenue, street by street, the lines in his map are perfectly straight without the use of a ruler. I see him doing the same thing on the same subway bench the next day and admire his dedication. On the third day, it dawns on me that this young artist lives in the subway. At night, I see a group of grinning people walking around with grabbers, searching for litter on the sidewalk. “We’re just helping clean up the neighborhood,” one of them tells me. “Oh, that’s so nice of you,” I say, feeling genuinely impressed. But then I notice that everyone is suspiciously good-looking and that there’s barely any litter to pick up. It appears that the members of this “trash club” are here to pick up more than just trash.  A flock of birds in the sky makes the shape of a middle finger, reminding me it’s migration season. At the pierogi place, not a single soul is Polish. Global Wealth Clothing sells garments to the poor. The Cathedral of Joy is in a miserable spot. A place called The Community is empty of people. And on one of the windows of a shiny new building, a sign reads in big letters: "Warning: rat infestation. Tenants on rent strike."—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chiefPS—If you’re in New York on September 30, come meet me at the International Studio & Curatorial Program, where we’ll talk to resident artists and enjoy some refreshments. 

	
		
		Alfredo Jaar Is Still Trying to Change the World
		
	
	
		In April of 1987, when Reaganism was running amok and Henry Kissinger was fiddling with world affairs like a puppet master from hell, a relatively unknown 31-year-old Chilean artist named Alfredo Jaar staged his billboard installation A Logo for America smack dab in the heart of Times Square. It instantly became one of the most discussed works of political art in the contemporary canon. 

Appearing between ads for tomato sauce and a Mexican restaurant, the 42-second LED animation bewildered New Yorkers with the message “This Is Not America” superimposed on a map of the United States, followed by an image of the US flag with the text, “This Is Not America’s Flag.” Next, the “R” in America shifted into a dancing map of South, Central, and North America. | Hakim Bishara

title: Visitors Arrested at Louvre After Posting Their Artworks Near Mona Lisa
description: Two visitors to the Louvre in Paris were arrested Saturday after they installed two paintings in the Salle des États, which houses the Mona Lisa, ac
body:
Two visitors to the Louvre in Paris were arrested Saturday after they installed two paintings in the Salle des États, which houses the Mona Lisa, according to a report by Agence France-Presse that cited police sources.

	According to police, they stuck two paintings (each measuring about 11.8 by 15.7 inches) onto the walls of the Salle des États with sticky tape. One painting showed one of the suspects wearing a suit of armor, while the other showed the two with a woman. The Mona Lisa, which attracts crowds from opening to close, was not damaged in the incident.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	The two visitors were not identified by first name and last name initial, as is common in France, but only as German nationals. They were first detained by the Louvre’s security team before being arrested for damaging the museum’s walls; they told police they did it for fun, AFP reports.

	The Louvre did not immediately respond to ARTnews’s request for comment.

	Museums in France—and elsewhere in Europe—have been on high alert for the past year because thieves have taken valuable objects from their walls, not because visitors have added inconsequential ones to them. Nearly a year ago, the Louvre itself was the subject of a major heist in which $102 million worth of crown jewels were stolen in broad daylight from the Galerie d’Apollon, not far from the Mona Lisa. A series of thefts at various museums has followed in the wake.

	Shortly after the Louvre heist, a government audit leaked saying that the museum’s security system was “outdated and inadequate” and that there had been “repeated postponements of the scheduled modernization of security systems.” In the fallout, Laurence des Cars, the first woman to serve as president-director of the Louvre, resigned in February and was replaced the following day by Christophe Leribault.

	Over the summer, Leribault told the French Senate that the Louvre is “at the end of its ropes” because “urgent building issues are piling up, and we are facing a massive investment challenge.” He added that the museum is addressing “the necessary emergencies head-on,” which include its security; a new video surveillance system around the perimeter is to be installed in January.
	

	The Louvre will soon undergo a major renovation that is expected to cost more than €1 billion ($1.2 billion). The purpose is to ease the overcrowding of the museum and the construction of a new 33,000-square-foot exhibition space of Mona Lisa, which will have its own entrance. The plans were briefly put on pause earlier this year before being resumed, with the Louvre finally naming the architecture team to realize the renovation, called the “New Louvre Renaissance,” in May.

title: Liu Wei’s Cut-Up and Reassembled Sculptures Take Over the Met Museum’s Facade
description: A series of hybrid sculptures now gesture from the facade of New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In Speculation / Λ (2026), a black sphere acts a
body:
A series of hybrid sculptures now gesture from the facade of New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art. In Speculation / Λ (2026), a black sphere acts as the support for a hand that extends upward, as if trapped in a ruin of bone tissue, while in Speculation / G (2026), an outstretched hand lies at the base of a tower of protruding nails, rawhide, and layered geometric metal cutouts. Conceived of by Liu Wei and unveiled Thursday, the works range from nearly 9 feet tall to over 16 feet tall. Imposing in scale, they look like a group of anti-monuments when seen together.
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Fabricated in a range of materials, including rawhide, resin, fiberglass composite, bronze, aluminum alloy, steel, each mixed-media sculpture feels fragmented and unstable, its final form a chimera of different origins: biological, technological, architectural. “I want them to feel like objects born out of a wasteland,” Liu told me during a visit to his Beijing studio in June.

	At one point during my second visit, while we sat by his computer to look at the studies for these complex sculptures, his mouse stopped working. He took it as an opportunity to talk about the genesis of his artmaking. He began using computers right after he graduated from the China Academy of Art in 1996; an early machine that he built around 2000 had four drives working simultaneously. On it, he spent over a month piecing together a massive composite image of pictures from urban life. “I remember finishing it at 5 a.m., and then the system crashed,” he said. “I couldn’t sleep after that. I was going out of my mind.”

	His computer has been upgraded since, but his process remains the same. For the Met commission, he layered image upon image, piecing together collages against a digital photo of the museum’s facade in Photoshop, before translating them into small 3D maquettes. He objects to sending a blueprint to a fabricator. “That would turn it into a commodity,” he said matter-of-factly. For the Met project, he worked with a team of 13 assistants and specialists, who weren’t given strict instructions. “I give them a framework, then review and adjust things later,” he said. “It’s not about adhering to a preconceived, complete image.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Liu Wei, Speculation / ∧, 2026, installation view, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. 
									Photo Hyla Skopitz/Courtesy The Metropolitan Museum of Art
	



	Over the summer, during my first visit to Liu’s studio, he had already scaled-up his maquettes using an oil-based clay to produce a cast. He had just marked out cut lines on the clay’s surface, where he planned to slice the model apart, then piece it back together using different materials, recalling a technique he’s been familiar with since childhood.

	Born in 1972, Liu came of an age when material abundance represented hope and manufacturing ramped up, with slab-style apartment blocks proliferating. His parents, both surgeons, moved around a lot and Liu would often get bored, turning to drawing to pass the time. Liu’s mother would influence her middle son’s future art career in another important way, buying him books and magazines about art, some of which introduced him to the work of figures like Diego Rivera and Andy Warhol.

	Even before he started university, Liu knew he wouldn’t continue oil painting, though that was his major and the prevailing aesthetic was still realism. His school surprisingly had a tradition of not being deferential to one’s professors; Liu recalled a teacher trying to bribe students with a pack of cigarettes to get them to attend class. The school was a cradle for avant-garde art in China: Yang Fudong was a year ahead of him, while video artist Zhang Peili had graduated from the oil painting department a decade earlier. Liu played soccer, drank, and skipped class. But after he graduated, unwilling to ask his parents for money, and, as he put it, “so broke I couldn’t afford lightbulbs,” he buckled down to work.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Liu Wei, Speculation / G , 2026, installation view, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. 
									Photo Hyla Skopitz/Courtesy The Metropolitan Museum of Art
	



	From 1998, Liu began to explore the conceptual approach of making an incision—creating something akin to a wound. He’d cut things out, photograph them, then manipulate the image. He applied this to readymades in his “Antimatter” series (2006) comprised of remixed appliances from the homes of migrant workers, who crafted these objects from whatever materials they could get their hands on. “I took them apart, cut them up, and put them back together, so that all their internal organs were exposed,” he said, noting that this process of disassembling and reassembling is meant to mimic capitalist modes of production.

	For Liu, artmaking has never really been about making something from scratch, but about responding to things that already exist, or as he says, “rethinking, re-examining, and discerning the nature of things.” When he visits institutions like the Met, the British Museum, or the Louvre, what interests him most, even beyond artistic qualities, is the context of a given work’s creation—what drove its maker to divine it.

	In our modern world, something that itself has been pieced together, he sees an analogue to his artistic approach. Technology, he said, has made an already fragmented society even more so, our sensory systems replaced by the latest gadget or app. “Society is all wrapped up, you can’t see anything,” he said. “We lose our physical sense of self, and, in reality, our capacity for emotion.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Liu Wei, Speculation / h, 2026, installation view, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. 
									Photo Hyla Skopitz/Courtesy The Metropolitan Museum of Art
	



	Liu is wary of offering a neat explication for his latest installations. He did share, however, that he likes the motif of spheres because they lack inherent directionality. He is personally drawn to hands for the sense of power they convey. “Hands carry so many meanings—creation, destruction, and everything in between,” he said. Speculation / h (2026) carries biological overtones, its shape recalling a human heart, to which he has grafted fingers that almost clutch the organ. But ultimately, for Liu, the initial concept ceases to matter; the act of constructing the image itself becomes more important than the starting point.

	From a distance, one side of Speculation / c (2026) looks like a premodern saint carved from rock, melted into a scream. On the other side, an index finger pointing straight to the sky suggests a warning, a call to attention. Liu’s Met commission, with its disembodied hands, its severing and suturing of the organic and the mechanical, may be a metaphor for a civilization detached from its foundations and coming to its end.


			
			
			
	
			
					Liu Wei, Speculation / c, 2026, installation view, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. 
									Photo Hyla Skopitz/Courtesy The Metropolitan Museum of Art
	



	The commission’s main constraint was spatial, as each sculpture had to fit into the narrow area between two columns, measuring about 8.5 feet width. “Limitations serve as a fulcrum,” he said of the challenge. “Without them, everything loses its power.”
	

	Even time is a limitation that Liu likes to work up against. He continued fine-tuning the sculptures right up until they were crated for shipping to New York. One of his biggest alterations, which came late in the process, were to the nails on the hands. He cut them off, made new molds, and attached them once more. He was constantly confronting the works as physical objects. “It’s much like how people are formed,” Liu said. “Just as we navigate society and encounter various forces, those experiences constantly shape who we are.”
